FOR REVERB SELLERS

See whether that offer still beats eBay.

Enter the rates from your last Reverb payout and the eBay final-value fee you actually pay. The calculator shows cash at your list price, cash if you take the offer, and the Reverb offer that leaves the same cash as selling the same item on eBay. Walk the numbers on should I take this Reverb offer, then use "Copy counter-offer message" below to paste a reply naming the crossover price straight into your Reverb inbox. Declining it does not buy a guaranteed sale at list — it buys a chance of one — so price that bet on should I wait for a better Reverb offer. A bump is cash out of this sale — compare it to taking the offer on should I bump this Reverb listing. Marketplace fee sits on the item, so baking postage into the list costs extra — compare that to charging shipping, absorbing the label, or offering pickup on should I include shipping on Reverb and should I eat the shipping. Reverb Safe Shipping is a more expensive label, not a different checkout — compare it to your own label on should I buy Reverb Safe Shipping. A shop that will consign or buy the guitar today is a different sale — compare that on should I consign this Reverb listing. And when a buyer opens a case, the freight runs three legs and the piece comes back worth less — see the largest concession that still beats the return on should I take the return or refund part of it. See how this differs from Reverb's own Selling Fees page and Earnings breakdown on this calculator vs. Reverb's own tools, or from tracking these seven decisions in a spreadsheet on this calculator vs. a spreadsheet.

Numbers stay in this browser. The shareable link puts them in the URL. This is arithmetic on your inputs, not Reverb's or eBay's live fee schedule. Payment processing defaults to Reverb's standard-seller rate (3.19% + $0.49, per Reverb's own Selling Fees page as of September 2026) — Preferred Sellers pay 2.99% + $0.49 instead, so overwrite the field if that is you. The marketplace fee cap defaults to $500 — Reverb's own published ceiling on the selling fee itself, for standard and Preferred sellers alike, so a $15,000 guitar owes $500 rather than the uncapped 5% ($750). It only changes the number above roughly $10,000 at a 5% rate; set it to 0 if your plan has no cap. Rates change; check Reverb's own Selling Fees page before trusting either default.

Offer versus list, Reverb versus eBay

Path Sale price Fees Net cash vs Reverb list

Marketplace and Reverb Gives apply to the item price. Payment processing applies to item plus shipping charged. eBay's final-value fee in this compare applies to item plus shipping, the usual marketplace shape — overwrite it from your own statement.

Take the offer now, or wait for a better one?

Path Chance Sale price Net cash vs taking it now

Declining an offer does not buy a sale at list — it buys a chance of one, and otherwise the realistic alternative is usually another offer near (or below) the one already in hand. Type your own odds of eventually reaching list and what you expect to settle for if you don't; the two rows and the break-even chance above update.

Buyer-pays, include shipping, absorb the label, or pickup

Path Buyer checkout Fees Net cash vs buyer-pays

Including shipping folds postage into the item so marketplace fee rises. Absorbing the label keeps your typed list and leaves the postage on you — a cheaper checkout for the buyer and less cash for you. Local pickup uses your list with no shipping charged; add gas or parking as the meetup cost if pickup is not free. This is not a recommendation — it is the arithmetic on the rates you typed. Include-shipping example. Absorb-the-label example.

Your own label or Reverb Safe Shipping

Path Label you pay Expected claim Expected net vs own after claims

Safe Shipping does not change what the buyer pays. It only changes the label you buy and whether you eat a damaged or lost shipment. Expected keep subtracts (claim rate × cash you lose on an unprotected claim) from own-label profit. A $0 Safe Shipping quote is illustrated at your own label plus $15 so the table is never empty. This is not a recommendation to buy their label — it is the arithmetic on the rates you typed. Worked example.

List it yourself, consign at the shop, or take their cash

Path Their price You receive Net after gear vs Reverb list

Consignment is a percent of the shop's sale, not of your Reverb list. They ship and they collect, so this path does not pay Reverb marketplace, payment processing, a bump, or a label. Their cash offer is a buy today — you walk with that number minus what you paid for the gear. This is not a recommendation to consign or to take their cash — it is the arithmetic on the rates you typed. Worked example.

Pay for a bump, or take the offer

Path Sale price Fees Net cash vs offer, no bump

A bump is a fixed cash out of this sale. Paying one and still taking the same offer always leaves less by exactly the bump. It only pays if it gets you to list or to a higher offer that covers the bump after percentage fees. A $0 bump is illustrated at $3 so the table is not the same sale twice — overwrite it from your listing. This is not a recommendation to buy a bump. Worked example.

Take the return, or refund part of it and let them keep it

Path Cash back to buyer Fees credited Item back? Where you end up vs the return

A returned guitar is not a returned phone case. The freight runs three legs — out, back, and out again on the relist — the piece is one of one, so the cash you recover is whatever the relist fetches, and the card processor generally keeps its cut even when Reverb credits the selling fee. The 61% default is the selling fee's share of total fees on the worked example; read your own payout statement and overwrite it. Set the relist price to $0 for a piece that comes back unsellable. This is not a recommendation to refuse a return, and nothing here changes what Reverb's policies or your local law require of you. Worked example.

Common questions

Why doesn’t this know Reverb’s current fees?

On purpose. Every rate here is an input rather than a stored fee schedule, so the result is something you can check line by line against your own Reverb payout statement instead of a claim about what Reverb charges this month. Marketplace rates change, sellers land on different plans, and a stored table that has drifted is worse than no table — it looks authoritative and is quietly wrong. Type what your statement says and the arithmetic is yours.

Why is the marketplace fee on the item price but the payment fee on the total?

Because that is the usual shape: the marketplace cut (and Reverb Gives, if you have it on) applies to what the item sold for, while card processing applies to everything the buyer paid, shipping included. It matters more than it sounds. On the worked example — $800 plus $75 shipping — processing is charged on all $875, so shipping you charge is not fee-free revenue. If your own statement folds shipping into the marketplace line instead, raise the marketplace rate or put the difference in the other-cost field.

Does an $80 discount cost me $80?

No, and that is the useful part of the offer comparison. Dropping the worked example from $800 to $720 takes profit from $281.60 to $208.15 — $73.45, not $80 — because the marketplace and processing fees fall with the price too. It cuts both ways: a low offer still costs you most of the discount, so the tool shows what is left rather than whether the offer “feels” fair.

Does the marketplace fee really stop growing on an expensive item?

Yes — Reverb caps its own selling fee at $500 per sale, for standard and Preferred sellers alike, per Reverb’s own Selling Fees and Preferred Seller help pages. A $15,000 guitar owes $500, not the uncapped 5% of $750. Below roughly $10,000 at a 5% rate the cap never binds and this changes nothing; above it, every comparison on this page — offer vs list, vs eBay, vs a shop — uses the capped number. Reverb Gives and payment processing are not capped, only the marketplace line. If your plan has no cap, set the field to 0.

Am I better off on Reverb or eBay?

On the same sale it depends almost entirely on the fee rates you type. With the worked example’s defaults Reverb’s fees come to $68.40 against eBay’s $119.40 at a 13.6% final value rate, so Reverb keeps about $51 more of the same $875. Put your actual rates in before you trust the direction — the point of the comparison is that a category rate and a promoted-listing rate can flip it.

Is Reverb Safe Shipping worth the extra label cost?

That is an expected-value question, not a preference, and the tool answers it that way. The worked example pays $15 more for the protected label against a $450 claim exposure, so the break-even is a 3.33% loss rate: below that, self-insuring wins on average; above it, the protected label does. At the default 2% the expected claim is $9 and own-label comes out $6 ahead. Two honest caveats the arithmetic cannot carry: your real loss rate on vintage or fragile pieces may be well above your average, and expected value says nothing about whether you could absorb one $450 hit this month.

How should I think about a return?

As three legs of freight, not one. The piece ships out, comes back, and ships out again on the relist; it is one of one, so what you recover is whatever the relist actually fetches; and the card processor generally keeps its cut even where the selling fee is credited. That last part is the 61% default — the selling fee’s share of total fees on the worked example, which you should overwrite from your own payout statement. Set the relist price to $0 for something that comes back unsellable. None of this is advice to refuse a return, and it does not change what Reverb’s policies or your local law require of you.

Is my data uploaded anywhere?

No account and no network requests — the calculator runs entirely in your browser. The shareable link carries your numbers in the URL itself rather than sending them to a server, so whoever you send it to sees the same scenario without anything being stored. The optional usage counter records only which features were used and the day, never your prices, costs, or margins.

Should I take this offer or wait for a better one?

That depends on a probability this tool cannot know for you: how often gear like yours, at your asking price, actually reaches list. On the worked example — $720 offer, $800 list, and a fallback of $680 if list is not reached — taking the offer now leaves $208.15 for certain. Waiting only pays in expectation once your real chance of reaching list clears 33.33%; below that, the certain $208.15 beats the probability-weighted average of a $281.60 list sale and a $171.43 fallback. Type your own odds and fallback price on the calculator — this is the arithmetic of a bet, not a claim about how often you personally will win it.

← Reverb fee calculator

Should I bump this Reverb listing?

A used guitar is listed at $800. A $720 offer is in the inbox. You paid $450 for the guitar and $10 to set it up. Shipping is $75 charged / $65 you pay. Reverb marketplace is entered at 5% of the item, payment at 3.19% + $0.49. Bump fee on the listing is $0, so the table uses a $3 illustration — a typical Reverb bump, not a live price. Overwrite it on the calculator.

A bump is a fixed cash out of this sale. It never pays on the same price. Paying $3 and still taking $720 always leaves $3 less. It only pays if it gets you from that offer to list — or to an offer high enough to cover the bump after marketplace and payment take their cut.

PathSale priceFeesNet cashvs offer, no bump
Take the offer, no bump$720.00$61.85$208.15+$0.00
Take the offer, pay the bump$720.00$64.85$205.15−$3.00
Sell at list, no bump$800.00$68.40$281.60+$73.45
Sell at list, pay the bump$800.00$71.40$278.60+$70.45

On this example, a $3.00 bump still pays if it gets you from the $720 offer to the $800 list — you keep $70.45 more than taking the offer with no bump. To keep no-bump offer cash after paying the bump, you need $723.27 ($3.27 more after percentage fees).

Waiting for list with no bump still leaves the most cash. None of those sentences is advice to buy a bump or refuse an offer — they are the arithmetic on the inputs above.

Type your own bump fee on the calculator and the four paths update. Your numbers stay in the browser. Offer versus list is a different question — walk that on should I take this Reverb offer. Shipping included versus buyer-pays is on should I include shipping on Reverb. Comparing this guitar to eBay, Etsy, Amazon, or your own store? The where-to-sell calculator ranks Reverb against them with this item's price, shipping, and cost already filled in.

Common questions

Should I bump a Reverb listing or take the offer?

On the worked example — $800 list, $720 offer, $450 gear cost, 5% marketplace, 3.19%+$0.49 payment — taking the offer with no bump leaves $208.15. Paying a $3 bump and still taking $720 leaves $205.15. Selling at list with no bump leaves $281.60. Selling at list after the $3 bump leaves $278.60, which is $70.45 more than taking the offer. The bump only pays if it changes the price you take.

How much higher does a Reverb offer need to be to cover a bump?

Marketplace, payment, and Reverb Gives still take a cut of any higher offer. On the worked example a $3 bump needs $3.27 more item price, so $723.27 keeps the same cash as the $720 offer with no bump. Type your own bump on the calculator; this page does not claim Reverb's live bump prices.

Does a Reverb bump pay if I still take the same offer?

No. A bump is a fixed cash out of this sale. Paying one and still taking the same offer always leaves less by exactly the bump. It only pays if it gets you to list or to a higher offer that covers the bump after percentage fees.

should-i-buy-reverb-safe-shipping.html.text:
← Reverb fee calculator

Should I buy Reverb Safe Shipping?

A used guitar is listed at $800 plus $75 shipping. Your own label is $65. Reverb quotes $80 for Safe Shipping. You paid $450 for the guitar. If a shipment is damaged or lost without their protection, you eat that $450. You expect that on 2% of the labels you buy yourself. Reverb marketplace is entered at 5% of the item, payment at 3.19% + $0.49 on item plus shipping charged. These are starting points, not live schedules — overwrite them on the calculator.

Safe Shipping does not change the $875 checkout. It only changes the label you buy and whether you eat the claim. Expected keep subtracts $9.00 (2% of $450.00) from own-label profit. The extra $15.00 label is a sure cost; the claim is a maybe.

PathLabel you payExpected claimExpected netvs own after claims
Own label if nothing goes wrong$65.00$0.00$281.60+$9.00
Own label after expected claims$65.00$9.00$272.60+$0.00
Reverb Safe Shipping$80.00$0.00$266.60−$6.00

On this example, your own label still leaves the most expected cash. Safe Shipping's extra $15.00 label is worth it only if you lose more than 3.33% of shipments at a $450.00 claim. At a 4% claim rate the expected claim becomes $18.00 and Safe Shipping would leave $266.60 versus $263.60 on your own label.

None of those sentences is advice to buy or skip their label — they are the arithmetic on the inputs above. Enter the quote from the Reverb shipping screen and the cash you would actually lose on an unprotected claim (often replacement cost, sometimes a refunded sale).

Change the Safe Shipping quote, the claim cost, or the claim rate on the calculator and the three paths update. Your numbers stay in the browser. Who pays postage is a different question — walk that on should I include shipping on Reverb. Comparing this guitar to eBay, Etsy, Amazon, or your own store? The where-to-sell calculator ranks Reverb against them with this item's price, shipping, and cost already filled in.

Common questions

Should I buy Reverb Safe Shipping or use my own label?

On the worked example — $800 list, $75 shipping charged, $65 own label, $80 Safe Shipping quote, $450 gear cost as the unprotected claim, 2% claim rate, 5% marketplace, 3.19%+$0.49 payment — your own label leaves $281.60 if nothing goes wrong and $272.60 after the $9.00 expected claim. Safe Shipping leaves $266.60. The extra $15.00 label is worth it only if you lose more than 3.33% of shipments at a $450.00 claim.

Does Reverb Safe Shipping change what the buyer pays?

No. Safe Shipping changes the label you buy and whether you eat a damaged or lost shipment. Marketplace and payment fees stay the same when the buyer still pays the same shipping charged. Who pays postage — buyer, included, or pickup — is a different question.

When does Reverb Safe Shipping beat my own label?

When the expected unprotected claim (claim rate times cash you lose on a damaged or lost shipment) is larger than the extra label cost. On the worked example that crossover is 3.33%. A $0 Safe Shipping quote is illustrated at your own label plus $15.00 so the table is never empty.

should-i-consign-this-reverb-listing.htm.text:
← Reverb fee calculator

Should I consign this Reverb listing?

A used guitar is listed on Reverb at $800 plus $75 shipping. You paid $450 for it. Marketplace is entered at 5% of the item, payment at 3.19% + $0.49 on item plus shipping charged, postage you pay at $65, and $10 of packing. A local shop will consign it at 30% of an $800 sale, or buy it today for $520. These are starting points, not live schedules — overwrite them on the calculator.

Consignment is a percent of the shop's sale. They ship and they collect, so you do not pay Reverb marketplace, payment processing, a bump, or a label. Their cash offer is a buy today. Listing it yourself keeps the Reverb checkout and the fees that come with it.

PathTheir priceYou receiveNet after gearvs Reverb list
List it yourself on Reverb$800.00$731.60$281.60+$0.00
Consign at the shop$800.00$560.00$110.00−$171.60
Take their cash offer today$520.00$520.00$70.00−$211.60

On this example, listing it yourself still leaves the most cash. A 30% shop cut on an $800.00 sale leaves $171.60 less than Reverb at list, and $98.15 less than taking the $720.00 Reverb offer ($208.15). The shop cut would have to drop to 8.55% — or they would have to sell it at $1045.14 — to match Reverb list cash. Their cash offer would have to be $731.60.

At a 15% shop cut the consignment payout becomes $680.00 and net after gear is $230.00. That still loses to the $281.60 Reverb list, but it beats the $208.15 Reverb offer by $21.85.

None of those sentences is advice to consign, to take their cash, or to keep the listing — they are the arithmetic on the inputs above. Enter the cut the shop actually quoted and the cash they would hand you today.

Change the shop sale price, the consignment cut, or the cash offer on the calculator and the three paths update. Your numbers stay in the browser. Who pays postage is a different question — walk that on should I include shipping on Reverb. Comparing this guitar to eBay, Etsy, Amazon, or your own store? The where-to-sell calculator ranks Reverb against them with this item's price, shipping, and cost already filled in.

Common questions

Should I consign a guitar or list it myself on Reverb?

On the worked example — $800 Reverb list, $75 shipping charged, $65 postage you pay, $450 gear cost, 5% marketplace, 3.19%+$0.49 payment, $800 shop sale, 30% shop cut, $520 cash offer — listing it yourself leaves $281.60. Consigning leaves $110.00. Their cash offer leaves $70.00. The shop cut would have to drop to 8.55%, or they would have to sell it at $1045.14, to match Reverb list cash. Their cash offer would have to be $731.60.

Does a shop consignment pay Reverb fees?

No. The shop ships and collects. You receive their sale price minus their cut, then subtract what you paid for the gear. Marketplace, payment processing, a bump, and a label stay on the self-list path.

When does taking the shop's cash beat listing on Reverb?

When their cash offer minus what you paid for the gear is larger than Reverb list profit on the rates you typed. On the worked example that crossover is $731.60. A $520 cash offer leaves $70.00 versus $281.60 on Reverb.

Local pickup$800.00$273.99−$7.61

Shipping included in the price$875.00$72.15$277.85−$3.75
Local pickup$800.00$66.01$273.99−$7.61

Local pickup leaves −$7.61 versus charging shipping, because you give up $75 of shipping charged to save $65 of postage and a little payment fee. To keep buyer-pays cash with shipping included, list at $879.08.

Pickup can still win when the postage you pay is larger than what you charge, or when shipping charged is already zero. Keeping the $800 list and absorbing the label is a fourth path — walk that on should I eat the shipping. Should I include shipping on Reverb or charge the buyer?

Local pickup uses your list with no shipping charged and no postage you pay. On the worked example that leaves $273.99 versus $281.60 if the buyer pays $75 shipping and you spend $65 to ship. Should I take the return or refund part of it on Reverb?

A guitar sold for $800. Shipping charged was $75 and the outbound label cost $65. You paid $450 for it and $10 to set it up. Now the buyer says the finish has a check you did not photograph, and asks to send it back. The return label would be $75. If it comes back you would relist it at $720, because a piece that has shipped twice with a claim opened does not fetch the first price. Overwrite any of that on the calculator.

PathCash back to buyerFees creditedItem back?Where you end upvs the return
Sale stands, no adjustment$0.00$0.00no$281.60+$250.42
Partial refund, they keep it$150.00$7.10no$138.70+$107.53
Take the return, relist it$875.00$41.43yes$31.17+$0.00
Full refund, they keep it$875.00$41.43no−$551.98−$583.15

Taking the return leaves $31.17 against $281.60 if the sale stands. The return costs $250.42, and the three pieces of that are worth naming separately, because a fee schedule shows you none of them:

  • $205.00 of freight over three legs. $65 out, $75 back, $65 out again on the relist. On a Strat in a gig bag this is annoying; on a 2×12 combo it is most of the decision.
  • $26.98 of fees no refund gives back. Reverb credits the selling fee on the percentage lines only; the fixed $0.49 per-order payment fee is never refund-linked, and the card processor generally keeps its variable cut too. On these rates that is $26.98 of the $68.40 charged, and it is charged whether the guitar comes back or not.
  • $73.45 given up on the relist. The piece is one of one. There is no second unit on the shelf, so the cash you recover is whatever the relist fetches — $208.15 net at $720, against the $281.60 the original sale would have left.

The number that actually decides it

So the useful question is almost never "return or no return". It is how big a concession is still cheaper than the return. Every dollar you refund costs a dollar less the fee credit it earns back, so the break-even is grossed up by that keep rate. On these inputs it is $262.87 — 32.9% of the sale price.

Read that plainly: you could knock $263 off an $800 guitar, let the buyer keep it, and still end up ahead of taking it back. The $150 you were thinking of offering leaves $107.53 more than the return. A full refund with the buyer keeping the guitar does not — that is $583.15 worse, because you are out the cash and the instrument both.

When the arithmetic flips

Two inputs move this more than the fee rates do. Relist price is the first: set it to $0 for a piece that comes back unsellable, and the return costs $908.57 rather than $250.42 — at that point even refunding the whole order and letting them keep it beats shipping it back. Return shipping is the second: if the buyer pays it, drop it to $0 and the return costs $75 less. Which of those applies depends on why the case was opened, and that is a fact about your order, not something a calculator can know.

None of these sentences is advice to refuse a return, to make an offer, or to argue a case. They are the arithmetic on the inputs above. What Reverb's policies and your local consumer law require of you is a separate question, and it is not one this tool answers — a return you are obliged to accept is not made optional by being expensive. The number is useful for the case where you have a choice: what to offer, and how far you can go before shipping it back is genuinely cheaper.

Marketplace and Reverb Gives apply to the item. Payment processing applies to item plus shipping charged, and its fixed per-order line is never refunded. The 61% fee-credit default is the selling fee's share of total fees on this example — read your own payout statement and overwrite it, along with every other rate. Your numbers stay in the browser. A different question — whether a buyer's offer is worth taking in the first place — is on should I take this Reverb offer, and whether to buy the insured label that prevents some of these cases is on should I buy Reverb Safe Shipping. Comparing this guitar to eBay, Etsy, Amazon, or your own store? The where-to-sell calculator ranks Reverb against them with this item's price, shipping, and cost already filled in.

Common questions

Should I take the return or refund part of it on Reverb?

On the worked example — $800 sale, $75 shipping charged, $65 outbound label, $75 return label, $450 item cost, $10 prep, 5% marketplace, 3.19%+$0.49 payment, 61% of fees credited on a refund, $720 relist — letting the sale stand leaves $281.60 and taking the return leaves $31.17. The return costs $250.42: $205.00 of freight over three legs, $26.98 of processing no refund gives back, and $73.45 given up on the relist. Any partial refund up to $262.87 — 32.9% of the sale price — leaves more than shipping it back. None of that is advice to refuse a return, and it does not change what Reverb's policies or your local law require.

Why is a Reverb return worse than a return on a marketplace of commodity goods?

Three reasons, and all three are specific to used gear. The freight runs three legs rather than one — out, back, and out again on the relist — and each leg on a combo amp or a hardshell case is real money. The piece is one of one, so there is no second unit on the shelf: the cash you recover is whatever the relist fetches, and something that has shipped twice with a claim opened rarely fetches the first price. And Reverb credits the selling fee on a refund while the card processor generally keeps its cut, so a residue is charged whether the buyer keeps the item or ships it back.

Should I wait for a better Reverb offer?

A used guitar is listed at $800. A buyer offers $720. You paid $450 for the guitar and $10 to set it up. Shipping is $75 charged / $65 you pay. Reverb marketplace is entered at 5% of the item, payment at 3.19% + $0.49. Declining the offer does not buy a sale at $800 — it buys a chance of one. Type your own odds and fallback on the calculator; this worked example uses a 30% chance of eventually reaching list, and $680 as the price you would realistically settle for otherwise.

PathChanceSale priceNet cashvs taking it now
Take the offer now100%$720.00$208.15+$0.00
Wait, eventually reach list30%$800.00$281.60+$73.45
Wait, eventually settle for less70%$680.00$171.43−$36.72

At a 30% chance of eventually reaching list — else settling near $680.00 — taking the $720.00 offer now still leaves $3.67 more in expectation than waiting. The break-even chance of eventually reaching list is 33.33%: below that, the certain $208.15 in hand beats the probability-weighted average of a better sale and a worse one; above it, waiting comes out ahead.

None of those sentences is advice to accept or refuse the offer, or a claim about your actual odds of reaching list — they are the arithmetic on the odds and prices you type. Nobody but the seller has a defensible number for "how often gear like this actually reaches list at this asking price," and this tool does not pretend to know it.

Every other comparison on this calculator treats "wait for list" as a sure thing. This is the one place it isn't. Offer versus a certain list sale is a different question, walked on should I take this Reverb offer. Whether a bump pays is on should I bump this Reverb listing. Your numbers stay in the browser. Comparing this guitar to eBay, Etsy, Amazon, or your own store? The where-to-sell calculator ranks Reverb against them with this item's price, shipping, and cost already filled in.

Common questions

Should I wait for a better Reverb offer?

On the worked example — $720 offer, $800 list, $450 gear cost, 5% marketplace, 3.19%+$0.49 payment, a 30% typed chance of eventually reaching list and a $680 fallback price otherwise — taking the offer now leaves $208.15 for certain. Waiting leaves $204.48 in expectation (30% x $281.60 list, 70% x $171.43 fallback), which is $3.67 less. The break-even chance of eventually reaching list is 33.33%: below that, taking the offer wins on average; above it, waiting does.

What is the break-even chance of reaching list?

The probability of eventually selling at list that makes the expected value of waiting exactly equal to taking the offer in hand. On the worked example it is 33.33%. If your honest odds of reaching this exact list price are lower than that, the offer in hand is worth more in expectation even though it feels like leaving money on the table.

Why does the fallback price default below the offer?

Because an inbox that produced one lowball tends to produce more of them, and a "just wait for list" instinct usually assumes the next offer will be at least as good as the last one. It might not be. The calculator does not require the fallback to be lower than the offer in hand — type your own number — but defaulting it there keeps the illustration honest about the downside of holding out.

Is a 90%-of-asking offer on Reverb a lowball, or typical?

Reverb's own Making Offers guidance says an offer under roughly 65% of the asking price is auto-rejected by its Lowball Offer Policy before a seller ever sees it, and that most accepted offers land between about 70% and 95% of asking. The $720 offer against the $800 list on this page is 90% of asking — inside that typical band, not the kind of lowball Reverb already filters out. That says nothing about whether taking it beats waiting on this seller's own odds of a better offer; it only says the offer itself is not unusual.

vs-reverbs-selling-fees-page.html.text:
← Reverb fee calculator

This calculator vs. Reverb's own Selling Fees page

Reverb publishes its seller rate schedule on a Selling Fees page, detailed further in its help center: a 5% selling fee on the item price plus shipping (minimum $0.50, maximum $500 in USD), and a Reverb Payments processing fee of 3.19% + $0.49 per transaction for standard sellers, or 2.99% + $0.49 for Preferred Sellers, on the order total. A cross-border order can add roughly 1%, and listing in a different currency than your payout currency can add a 2.5% conversion fee. That schedule is free to any seller and is the right place to check what a rate currently is.

After a sale, Reverb's own Earnings page in a seller's account itemizes exactly what was withheld from that payout — a real, useful, and free resource, but a retrospective one: it tells you what a sale already cost, not what a choice in front of you will cost. Reverb's own help center carries an article on why total earnings look lower than the sale price, which is the question this calculator exists to answer before the sale happens rather than after.

Between those two resources — a schedule that states rates, and a statement that reports what already happened — sits the arithmetic on a decision still open: does a buyer's offer beat waiting for list, does the same item beat its Reverb number on eBay, is Reverb Safe Shipping worth the extra label after expected claims, does a shop's consignment cut or cash offer beat listing it yourself, does a bump still pay, and what does a partial refund cost against taking a return. This calculator does not try to reproduce Reverb's live rate card — every fee here is a box you type from your own statement, so it never drifts out of date the way a stored table would.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or Reverb's own Selling Fees page?

Both, for different jobs. Reverb's own Selling Fees page publishes the rate schedule sellers pay: a 5% selling fee on the item plus shipping, a Reverb Payments processing fee, and the rest of the free-to-any-seller schedule. It is the right place to check what a rate currently is. It does not compare a buyer's offer to waiting for list, does not weigh Reverb against selling the same item on eBay, does not price Safe Shipping against an unprotected label after expected claims, and does not check a shop's consignment cut or cash offer against listing it yourself. This calculator does not try to reproduce Reverb's rate schedule — every rate here is a box you type from your own statement — and instead answers the seven follow-on decisions the schedule itself leaves open.

Does Reverb have its own interactive fee calculator?

Reverb publishes two free resources, and neither is a standalone what-if calculator: a Selling Fees page stating the rate schedule before you list, and an Earnings page inside a seller's own account that itemizes what was withheld after a sale already happened. Reverb also publishes a help article explaining why total earnings can look lower than the sale price — evidence that the gap this calculator fills, seeing the net cash before you decide, is not something Reverb's own materials compute for you.

vs-tracking-offers-in-a-spreadsheet.html.text:
← Reverb fee calculator

Reverb Fee Calculator vs. tracking offers in a spreadsheet

A seller who works Reverb offers more than once usually ends up with a spreadsheet: a cell for the marketplace rate, one for payment processing, an eBay comparison built the same way from a second fee page, and a new tab whenever the situation changes shape — a Safe Shipping quote to weigh, a shop's consignment cut, a buyer asking for a partial refund instead of sending the item back. Each formula is ordinary arithmetic. Keeping seven of them in sync, across two marketplaces' own fee pages, as the situation changes under you, is the part that gets skipped when an offer needs an answer in the next five minutes.

What each approach actually does

A spreadsheet can reproduce every formula this calculator runs — offer versus list, Reverb versus eBay at the same price, Safe Shipping versus self-insuring a claim, a shop's cut versus their cash offer, a bump versus taking the offer as-is, and a partial refund versus a return. Building it means opening Reverb's fee schedule and eBay's separately, typing the right rate into the right cell, and adding a new section the next time the listing needs a decision the sheet does not already have — which used to mean opening two seller fee pages and a spreadsheet each time, per this tool's own README.

This calculator keeps all seven of those decisions on one screen already wired to the same marketplace and payment rates, so a lowball, a Safe Shipping quote, and a return request are the same worksheet instead of three. A shareable link carries the full scenario in the URL, and the where-to-sell handoff carries the item's price, shipping, and cost into a comparison against eBay, Etsy, Amazon, and an own store without retyping any of it.

QuestionWhere to answer it
What does this offer leave me versus waiting for list?This calculator's offer-vs-list panel — both prices, one screen.
Does the same item beat eBay at these prices?This calculator's Reverb-vs-eBay comparison, not a second fee page.
My situation has a wrinkle this calculator doesn't model (a bundle sale, a trade-in credit).A spreadsheet you build yourself — it can represent any rule you can describe.
I want to compare this item to eBay, Etsy, Amazon, or my own store too.The where-to-sell calculator, carried over with this item's numbers already filled in.
Is my data uploaded anywhere?No. Everything runs in your browser; your figures stay on this device.

Common questions

Can a spreadsheet do this math instead?

Yes. Every formula this calculator runs — offer versus list, Reverb versus eBay, Safe Shipping versus self-insuring, a shop cut versus a cash offer, a bump versus taking the offer, a partial refund versus a return — is ordinary arithmetic you can put in a spreadsheet. Getting there means opening Reverb's own fee schedule and eBay's separately, copying the right rate into the right cell, and rebuilding the sheet from scratch the next time a listing is a different shape (a case worth insuring, a consignment offer, a buyer asking for a partial refund instead of a return).

What does a spreadsheet not do that this calculator does?

Keep all seven decisions on one screen without re-deriving the sheet each time. A lowball, a Safe Shipping quote, and a return request rarely arrive on the same listing, so a spreadsheet built for one of them usually does not already have a row for the next one. This calculator also carries the item to the where-to-sell comparison with a link instead of retyping the price, shipping, and cost, and produces a ready-to-paste counter-offer message, which a formula cell does not.

Is a spreadsheet ever the better choice?

Yes, when your situation has a wrinkle this calculator does not model — a bundle of several items in one Reverb sale, a trade-in credited against the price, or a fee structure from a plan this tool's inputs cannot represent. A spreadsheet you build yourself can represent any rule you can describe. This calculator trades that flexibility for a form that already has the right fields for a single item moving through one of these seven decisions.

Is my data uploaded anywhere?

No. The calculator runs entirely in your browser. A shareable link carries your numbers in the URL itself rather than sending them to a server, and the optional usage counter records only which features were used and the day, never your prices or costs.
